content: Water softening involves the reduction of dissolved calcium, magnesium, manganese, and ferrous iron ions in hard water. A common water softener used for this purpose is sodium carbonate. These ions, often referred to as hardness ions, can cause several undesirable effects. Firstly, metal ions in hard water react with soaps and calcium-sensitive detergents, reducing their ability to lather and forming a precipitate, commonly known as bathtub ring. This reaction also diminishes the cleaning efficiency of detergents. Secondly, calcium and magnesium carbonates tend to precipitate out as hard deposits on surfaces such as pipes and heat exchangers. This phenomenon is primarily caused by the thermal decomposition of bicarbonate ions, although it can occur even in their absence. The accumulation of scale can restrict water flow in pipes and, in boilers, act as an insulating layer that reduces heat transfer efficiency. This can lead to overheating of metal boiler components and, in pressurized systems, may result in boiler failure. Thirdly, the presence of ions in an electrolyte, such as hard water, can lead to galvanic corrosion. This occurs when two different metals in contact with an electrolyte corrode at different rates, with one metal preferentially corroding. However, the sodium or potassium ions released during conventional water softening are more electrolytically active than the calcium or magnesium ions they replace. As a result, water softening can significantly increase galvanic corrosion rather than decrease it. Additionally, if lead plumbing is present, softened water is more likely to dissolve lead compared to hard water. Conventional household water-softening devices typically use ion-exchange resins. These resins contain negatively charged functional groups that bind positively charged metal ions. Initially, the resins are loaded with univalent hydrogen, sodium, or potassium ions, which are exchanged for divalent calcium and magnesium ions in the water. As water passes through the resin bed, the hardness ions replace the hydrogen, sodium, or potassium ions, which are then released into the water. The harder the water, the more ions are released from the resin into the treated water. Some resins are also designed to remove carbonate, bicarbonate, and sulfate ions, releasing hydroxyl ions in their place. Both types of resins can be combined in a single water softener. Over time, ion-exchange resins become saturated with undesirable cations and anions, losing their effectiveness. Regeneration is required to restore their functionality. For cationic resins, regeneration typically involves passing a concentrated brine solution, such as sodium chloride or potassium chloride, or a hydrochloric acid solution through the resin. For anionic resins, a solution of sodium or potassium hydroxide (lye) is used. Most of the salts used in regeneration are flushed out of the system and may be released into the environment, potentially causing harm, especially in arid regions. Some jurisdictions prohibit such discharges and require proper disposal of spent brine or the use of commercial services. To minimize environmental impact and conserve reagents, water softener manufacturers often provide metered control valves to reduce the frequency of regeneration and allow users to adjust the amount of reagent used. In industrial-scale water-softening plants, the effluent from the regeneration process can be significant. Under certain conditions, such as when the effluent mixes with domestic sewage, calcium and magnesium salts may precipitate as hardness scale inside discharge pipes, potentially leading to blockages. This issue was notably observed in a major chlor-alkali plant in South Wales during the 1980s. If potassium chloride is used instead of sodium chloride, the same ion-exchange process occurs, but potassium ions replace calcium, magnesium, and iron ions. This option is more expensive and may not be suitable for individuals on potassium-restricted diets. For individuals on low-sodium diets, the increase in sodium levels in softened water can be significant, particularly when treating very hard water. For example, a person consuming two liters of softened water with a hardness of 30 grains per gallon (gpg) would ingest approximately 480 mg more sodium than if they consumed unsoftened water. This amount is substantial, as the American Heart Association (AHA) recommends that individuals on severe salt-restricted diets consume no more than 400 mg of sodium per day, with no more than 10% of this intake coming from water. To address concerns about added sodium, many households install a bypass tap or a reverse osmosis unit for drinking and cooking water. Chelating agents are also used as water softeners and in various commercial products, such as shampoos and food preservatives. Citric acid is commonly employed to soften water in soaps and laundry detergents. A widely used synthetic chelating agent is EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid).
